name: memoization
intent: Cache the result of a pure function under a key derived from its arguments, so repeated calls with the same inputs return the stored result instead of recomputing it - trading memory for time.
problem: An expensive but deterministic function is called again and again with the same inputs - overlapping subproblems in a recurrence, the same rule at the same input position during backtracking, the same derived aggregate for an unchanged record - and every repetition pays the full cost even though the answer is already known.
context: Compute-bound code whose input sets recur: dynamic programming with overlapping subproblems, parsers and analysers that revisit the same state, expensive derivations from immutable data, per-object computed properties, and nullary initialisation inside a hot path. Preconditions are referential transparency (the call can be replaced by its return value) and a process that can afford to hold the results in memory; as soon as the cache is shared between threads, processes or tenants, the decision becomes a concurrency and scope decision rather than a pure optimisation.
benefits: Repeated calls collapse into one computation: exponential recurrences become polynomial (naive Fibonacci, edit distance, counting paths) and backtracking parsers stop re-parsing the same suffix.
The wrapped function keeps its signature and its call sites stay untouched, so the optimisation can be added, bounded or removed without a refactor.

No change of algorithm is required: any referentially transparent function can be memoized, including ones buried deep inside recursion, which is what makes it the standard first lever on an unexpected hot spot.
The trade is measurable: hit rate, miss count and current size are observable (functools cache_info, cache stores with metrics, profilers), so the cache can be kept or dropped on evidence.
Coordinates with lazy evaluation and pipelines: memoized sub-results can be computed on demand and reused by several downstream stages without extra machinery.

Acts as a correctness aid in some algorithms, not only a speed-up: memoizing rule/position pairs turns a backtracking parser into a linear-time one and makes previously exponential behaviour predictable.
tradeoffs: Space-time tradeoff with no natural bound: every distinct argument set is retained with its result, so memory grows with key cardinality and a long-running process needs a capacity limit, TTL or weak keys.

Sound only for referentially transparent functions: a function that reads mutable state, the clock, randomness, ambient configuration or I/O returns results that are stale the moment the world moves, and the memo silently hides that.

The result is only as good as the key: identity versus structural equality, argument order, self, mutable keys and unhashable argument types decide whether the cache hits, misses, collides or answers a different question.

Under concurrency a naive cache either computes the same key more than once, corrupts the store, or serializes every miss; the serialized forms can deadlock when the memoized function recurses through the same cache.

Hidden state changes observable behaviour: side effects of the wrapped function happen once, first-call latency differs from steady-state latency, and debugging observes a call history instead of a function.
The store owns its keys and values: entries prevent garbage collection, and results derived from a superseded configuration stay reachable until they are evicted or the process ends.
An in-process memo is invisible to other processes, hosts and restarts, so it is not a substitute for a cache layer when results must be shared or persisted.
A shared cache keyed only by caller-supplied values can serve one caller another caller's result when scope (tenant, user, authorisation) is missing from the key.

Cache stampede: when a hot key expires, many concurrent requests miss simultaneously and all hammer the underlying source before any result is written back - a naive memo offers no protection against this thundering-herd effect.

participants.responsibility: The referentially transparent function whose result is a pure function of its arguments; it may be recursive and must not depend on ambient mutable state.
Intercepts calls, derives the cache key from the arguments, and returns the stored result on a hit or delegates to the wrapped function on a miss and stores what it returns.
Holds key-result entries and provides the retrieval primitive: a plain map, a bounded LRU/TTL store, a weak-keyed table, or a concurrent map with an atomic compute-if-absent.
Defines what counts as the same inputs: hashing and equality of the argument list, structural versus identity comparison, and any extra context folded into the key (tenant, configuration, self).
Decides when entries leave the store: capacity bound with an eviction order, time-to-live, explicit clear or reset, or nothing at all for a process-lifetime memo over a bounded domain.

Makes concurrent misses safe when the memo is shared: one lock around the store, an atomic compute-if-absent, a once-cell for single values, or a documented decision to tolerate duplicate computation.

use_cases: Dynamic programming with overlapping subproblems: naive recursive Fibonacci, edit distance, knapsack, counting paths and coin-change variants, where memoization turns exponential recursion into linear or polynomial work.
Parsing and language tooling: packrat/memoizing parsers keyed on (rule, input position), attribute-grammar evaluation, and type or lattice joins that would otherwise re-derive the same node result.
Expensive derivations from immutable data: AST analyses, normalisations, geometry or financial computations keyed by a canonical argument struct that changes rarely but is asked for often.
Per-object computed properties: a record's derived aggregate, a configuration's parsed feature set, a decoded token payload - computed once and reused for the object's lifetime.
Nullary initialisation inside a hot path: lazily built lookup tables, compiled expressions, loaded indices or models that must be created once per process instead of once per call.
Pure helpers with a small, stable input domain on the server: unit and currency conversions, slug or locale normalisation, feature-flag evaluation against a fixed rule set, colour and geo lookups.

Request deduplication in web servers and APIs: when many concurrent requests arrive for the same resource, a single-flight or coalescing layer ensures only one upstream call fires while all requesters share the result - preventing a cache stampede at the exact moment a hot key expires.
Geolocation and geo-IP lookups: lat/lon to region, currency, language or regulatory-zone mapping from a fixed dataset, where the same coordinates or IP prefixes recur across many request handlers.

Certificate and key verification: parsing, validating chain-of-trust or checking revocation status for a fixed set of certificates, where the underlying certificate store changes infrequently relative to request frequency.
Feature-flag evaluation: resolving a user-context pair against a fixed rule set to produce a boolean or variant result, where the flag configuration is loaded once and queried many times.

Python's standard-library functools.cache and functools.lru_cache wrap pure, hashable-argument functions with unbounded or LRU memoization and expose cache_info/cache_clear for lifecycle and measurement.
Clojure's clojure.core/memoize returns a memoized function keyed by its arguments, providing a direct functional idiom for recursive or repeated pure computations.
Haskell's Data.Function.Memoize package supplies memoize, higher-arity memoize2/3/4, memoFix and finite-domain memoizeFinite, making the key/equality strategy explicit through Memoizable instances.
avoid_when: The computation is already cheap - a hash lookup, an arithmetic expression, a small string join: the wrapper, the key derivation and the retained memory cost more than the work they save.

The function is not referentially transparent: if it depends on mutable state, the clock, randomness, environment or I/O, a memo turns a stale value into a wrong answer; fix the dependency or pass the varying data in as an argument.
The value is needed once, or lives naturally for a single call - keep it in a local variable rather than in a cache.
Results must be shared across processes, hosts or restarts: use cache-aside/caching (Redis, CDN, HTTP cache) instead of process memory.

The concern is duplicate in-flight work rather than repeated calls over time: concurrent identical requests arriving together belong to singleflight / in-flight coalescing, which deliberately does not retain results for later callers.

The key domain is unbounded and caller-controlled (user ids, URLs, file paths) and no capacity limit or eviction policy is affordable: the memo becomes a memory-exhaustion vector, and a bounded cache with an explicit policy is the minimum.

The function is an async coroutine function: lru_cache stores the coroutine object returned on the first call; subsequent calls receive a different coroutine object and the cache silently returns the first one without awaiting, producing wrong results or deadlocks.
anti_patterns: Memoizing an impure function - time, randomness, mutable globals, request context - and treating a stale answer as a cache hit.
An unbounded per-process cache keyed by caller-controlled values used as if it were a cache-aside layer, in a process that also has a memory budget.
Caching a method without excluding or scoping self, so every instance's results - and with them every instance - stay alive for the process lifetime.
Keying on only part of the inputs, or on a repr/toString of the arguments, so distinct inputs share one entry and equal inputs land in different entries.
Creating the memo inside the call (a fresh cache per invocation) and expecting a speed-up.
Using the memo as concurrency control: deduplicating in-flight work with a result cache, or synchronising every miss on one lock until recursive calls deadlock.
Applying lru_cache to an async coroutine function and treating the cached coroutine object as a usable result.
Relying on cache hit rate as a correctness signal rather than as a performance metric - a cache can have 100% hit rate and serve entirely wrong answers.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the computation lives in the wrapped function, while keying, storage, eviction and synchronisation live in the wrapper.
Referential transparency as a precondition: the pattern is sound only when a call can be replaced by its return value.
Open/closed: adding a cache must not change call sites or the wrapped function's signature.
Single responsibility per collaborator: key derivation, storage and the retention policy are three separate decisions.
Explicit policy over implicit behaviour: capacity, expiry and invalidation are named in one place instead of being scattered across callers.
Measure before and after: a memo trades memory for time, so hit rate and footprint must be observable enough to justify it.

Cache stampede is a concurrency problem, not a caching problem: the memo must be paired with singleflight coalescing or probabilistic early refresh when the backing store is shared under concurrent load.
best_practices: Memoize only referentially transparent functions; if the result depends on ambient state, pass that state in as an explicit argument so it becomes part of the key.

Design the key deliberately: include everything the result depends on - all arguments plus tenant, configuration version or self where relevant - and decide explicitly between structural and identity equality.
Bound the cache whenever the key domain is unbounded (maxsize, LRU/TTL, size or weight limit) and keep the bound next to the construction of the store.
Choose the concurrency posture explicitly - single-owner, lock-protected, atomic compute-if-absent, or duplicate-tolerant - and check the recursion rules of the primitive you picked.
Give each cache a lifetime that matches its contents: per call, per instance, per process; clear or rebuild it on the event that changes the inputs.
Instrument hits, misses and size so the optimisation can be removed once it stops paying, and so cache misses are not mistaken for algorithm regressions.
Prefer weak or identity keys, or explicit removal, when the key set is the object graph itself (instances, nodes, DOM elements, parse nodes).

For time-sensitive data use a TTL-based cache (functools does not provide this natively; use the cachetools TTLCache or a handwritten decorator with time.monotonic timestamps) rather than an unbounded or purely LRU store.

When caching instance methods, store a per-instance lru_cache-wrapped function in __init__ (self.method = lru_cache(maxsize=N)(self._method_impl)) or use functools.cached_property for read-only properties - never apply lru_cache directly to a method definition, which attaches the cache to the class and retains every self instance indefinitely.

For async coroutine functions, use an explicit async-aware cache (a dict keyed by arguments plus asyncio.Lock or a dedicated library) rather than lru_cache; ensure the cache stores the resolved value, not the coroutine object.

Pair a memo with singleflight coalescing when concurrent identical requests can arrive simultaneously for an expensive miss: one computation runs while others wait and share the result (see oneflight, flightlock, coalescer Python packages, or Go's golang.org/x/sync/singleflight).
In distributed systems, add TTL jitter to prevent synchronized expiry waves across many processes sharing a Redis or Memcached backend.
Call cache_clear() explicitly after any mutation that invalidates the cached result; do not rely on TTL alone when correctness depends on invalidation rather than staleness tolerance.
For high-cardinality or caller-controlled key domains, consider a sliding-window or sampled eviction policy instead of pure LRU to prevent a single hot key from evicting useful entries.
Use typed=True on lru_cache when type differences in arguments imply semantic differences in the result (e.g. int vs float pixel coordinates), to avoid caching 1 and 1.0 under the same entry.

Expose cache_info() metrics to your observability stack (Prometheus, StatsD) and alert on hit rates below 50% - a cache consuming memory without saving measurable compute should be removed or resized.

Python documentation: functools — Higher-order functions and operations on callable objects. https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html — official reference for functools.cache, functools.lru_cache, cache_info, cache_clear, __wrapped__.

Vattani, A., Chierichetti, F. & Lowenstein, K. (2015). Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention. VLDB Endowment 8(8), 886-897 — the XFetch probabilistic early-expiration algorithm for preventing thundering-herd cache stampedes. https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.4456
Go singleflight: golang.org/x/sync/singleflight — the canonical in-flight request coalescing pattern that prevents thundering-herd on cache expiration in concurrent systems.
cachefence: probabilistic early refresh + distributed lock for Redis. https://github.com/bourne44/cachefence — implements XFetch + Redis rebuild-lock for stampede-free cache-aside.
oneflight: flexible sync and async singleflight for Python. https://github.com/dano/oneflight — per-key call coalescing with cancel-safe async support.
flightlock: single-flight cache stampede protection for Python. https://github.com/raoamogh/flightlock — per-key lock registry with TTL jitter and Redis backend support.

coalescer: collapse concurrent duplicate calls into a single execution — singleflight for asyncio and threads. https://github.com/roman-postnov/coalescer — covers ordering of cache outer vs coalescer inner decorators.

EngineersOfAI. 'Caching Strategies — Trading Memory for Speed.' https://engineersofai.com/docs/python/python-advanced/performance-engineering/caching-strategies — covers TTL caches, lru_cache gotchas, multi-layer caching, and event-driven invalidation.
